#1074. Rise of the ‘schooligans’: how a wave of antisocial behaviour threatens non-league football

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1621 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

Rise of the ‘schooligans’: how a wave of antisocial behaviour threatens non-league football

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1621 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Teenage ultras are increasingly causing disorder and communities fear it will not be long before it becomes something more dangerous.
  • It has been revealed that it is five past three on Saturday afternoon and the teenage ultras of Hednesford Town are running late.
  • The incident ended there and no one was hurt, though a police investigation has been debuted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Teenage ultras are increasingly causing disorder and communities fear it will not be long before it becomes something more dangerous.

It has been revealed that it is five past three on Saturday afternoon and the teenage ultras of Hednesford Town are running late. They have arrived in Chester for their team’s National League North fixture and have hailed taxis, determined to make their presence felt at the ground. But word appears to have got out about their arrival. As one car turns away from the city’s charming half-timbered houses and into narrow residential streets, half a dozen local youths appear, haring round the corner in balaclavas. They try to attack the cab and chase after it as it pulls away. The smell of pyro is everywhere. As the taxi finally gets clear, the Chester gang stops in the middle of the road, shouting and gesticulating. One lad, no older than 16, pulls a long blade from inside his trousers and brandishes it.

The incident ended there and no one was hurt, though a police investigation has been debuted. The match went off without trouble too and the Hednesford gang – known at home as the “schooligans” – were escorted safely back to the station by Cheshire police. It was just another weekend in English non-league football, where a wave of antisocial behaviour is causing concern and leading the UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) to declare it its “most vital” priority. As the disorder continues, a question remains: how long will it be before teenage trouble-making becomes something more dangerous?

This year clubs from the south coast to the north-east have reported disorder caused by supporters under the age of 18, some seemingly as young as 10. In February, Aldershot Town experienced a series of disorderly incidents involving young people that included brawls outside the ground, behaviour the club described as “wholly unacceptable and [which] will not be tolerated”. In August, Enfield Town noted they were “concerned and disappointed” by young fans at a fixture in Lewes. Two weeks ago, a Gloucester City fan was hit by a rock thrown by teenagers at Redditch United during an FA Trophy tie. Even Soham Town Rangers of the ninth-tier Eastern Counties League urged parents to ensure their children make “sensible choices” ahead of a match against Mildenhall Town.

Hednesford have experienced consistent trouble for a number of seasons and in August their owner and chair, Craig Gwilt, attempted to face it down. A rising tide of disorder was harming the club, he said, behaviour that included “pitch invasions, fighting, abuse directed towards players, missiles being thrown at opposition goalkeepers, flares entering the field of play and even interference with players’ water bottles”. He called on fans to improve their behaviour or risk permanently damaging the club. The plea was not immediately heard. Three weeks after Gwilt’s statement the club banned 20 young supporters from attending matches after there was action away at Telford.

Sources indicate that hednesford is a town of 19,000 people on the edge of the protected landscape of Cannock Chase. The town centre is neat and tidy, a well-maintained monument to the Stafford regiment at its heart. On the way to the ground you can get a pint at the Cross Keys where Dick Turpin reputedly rested his head. It’s a town seemingly at peace with itself and the club is at the heart of the community. But both are struggling to get to grips with an glitch that leaves people scratching their heads.

In a recent development, this season the club have introduced measures to prevent under-16s from entering without an accompanying adult. There is also extra security on matchdays, ostensibly to manage car parking. These interventions appear to have contained any trouble in and around the stadium, but now gangs of up to 50 youths will gather post-match at a safe remove to look for trouble or, more likely, save their energy for an away fixture. Like the one at Chester, for example, when the schooligans were removed from one train for antisocial behaviour and were drinking alcohol throughout their journey up. Encountering such groups on a Saturday will be familiar to many rail passengers.

The schooligans, whose nickname was coined by Hednesford’s security staff, “baffle” the club’s chief executive, Marvin Robinson, who would rather be spending his time modernising a club that have had back-to-back promotions. “I’m not really sure I understand why it seems to be a trend,” he says. “It’s a wider social issue but what is it and what will it become? Is it a social media thing? Is it about notoriety or becoming known for something? The adult response online has been almost to normalise it. I don’t agree with that.”.

Go on TikTok and the picture does start to become a little clearer. From aggregator accounts to individual semi-anonymised accounts belonging to the teenagers, there is a wealth of posts celebrating the behaviour of “top lads” who “mooch” to the ground before “running” the opposition out of town. Often set to a backing of euphoric electronic dance music with a layer or two of visual effects and captions such as “this weekend’s got me feeling like a little kid at Christmas”, the posts are celebratory and almost nostalgic in tone. In recent weeks TikTok has begun appending disclaimers to them that read: “Participating in this activity could result in you or others getting hurt.” TikTok removed an account named “NLN [National League North] gimps and chants”, when alerted to it by the Guardian, for contravening guidelines that do not allow content that glorifies violence.

Recent findings suggest that the mythology of old-school football hooliganism appears to be well‑known among these groups, with references to the 2005 film Green Street commonplace. But the schooligans of 2026 don’t behave like the firms of the past. For a start they rarely, if at all, arrange to fight their rivals. Instead they use the mapping feature on Snapchat to alert opposition to their presence on the day, and take it from there. The concept of rivalry itself is fluid. In the West Midlands, for example, teens from Hednesford will band together with those nominally affiliated with Redditch or Cannock Town. When there was trouble recently at Hednesford’s fixture at Hereford, local police said the majority of disorder had been caused by Redditch fans chasing supporters from Solihull Moors. It isn’t just local either. Children as young as 12 have been detained in the north-west having travelled from the south coast, a distance of more than 200 miles.

Industry observers note that the chair of Redditch, David Faulkner, is still dealing with the fallout from the Gloucester tie two weeks ago. He indicates the fluid set of alliances between ultra groups has created a “travelling circus” and that no one knows where it will turn up next. Branding himself “the non-League chair”, Faulkner has started posting videos on YouTube drawing attention to the disorder and calling for collective action.

It has been revealed that “People think of non-league football as one man and his dog, but we need to catch up with the fact that it’s massive now,” Faulkner states. “Some clubs have attendances bigger than in League One but the regulations were put in place decades ago. We need that extra regulation, that support, so we can get the funding to put things like CCTV and more stewarding in place. Because the other way this could go is that [change only happens] when someone gets seriously hurt. I haven’t got metal detectors on our gates to stop kids bringing knives in. None of that stuff. I’d rather take action before something happens.”.

The Football Association claims the behaviour of fans is primarily a matter for clubs and relevant authorities but that it is working to develop policies that welcome young fans safely to National League grounds. The UK Football Policing Unit, meanwhile, is working alongside leagues and the Crown Prosecution Service to develop fresh policies around “youth risk”, which are likely to include an extra focus on education via schools and community work.

“It’s probably the most key area of football policing that we’re focused on,” indicates Mike Ankers, the deputy director of the UKFPU. “We are seeing children as young as 12 or 13 engaged in antisocial behaviour at best, but also actual violence and that’s up and down the country, with some travelling hundreds of miles. There comes a great risk and a great safeguarding issue with regards to that. In terms of our focus, we are making sure that we bring the right people together to have a solution. It’s not just the policing, it requires a more holistic view.”.

According to recent reports, ankers indicates he supports Faulkner in speaking up on the topic and believes many more adults need to take responsibility. “These children need a strong adult role model,” he says. “I would very much question that if your 12-year-old is going out to follow football and is being detained, perhaps 200 miles away, then you need to look at how they’ve been able to travel and have those conversations. I think there’s very much a role for parental responsibility.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Hednesford schooligans, having been deposited on the platform at Chester by police, made their way home by train, only to find themselves stuck in a combination of Halloween revellers and national signal failure. Constrained, they hunched over their phones viewing footage from different teenage firms and discussed the day’s events. In the end, they concurred they had got the best of it. After all, noted one: “What experience do you get from chasing a taxi?”.

TikTok and Snapchat were approached for comment.

Arsenal make no sense – and defiant Mary Earps proves why

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Sources indicate that alone in an empty penalty box, Mary Earps dropped to her knees and yelled into the cold night air. With an eight-save, player-of-the-match display, the ‘Queen of Stops’ properly marked the end of her exile and return to the Women’s Super League with an outstanding performance between the posts for the London City Lionesses in their 1-1 draw with Arsenal, a reminder to anyone who needed it that the former England No 1 is not done yet.

Sources indicate that “Tiring,” Earps exhaled when asked to sum up a night where she did it all, including a sensational late stop to tip Frida Maanum’s dipping strike onto the bar and earn her side a point. There was agility, presence, bravery, but how about the timing, as well, to produce such a performance in front of the biggest crowd of the season at the Emirates and keep the disrupters London City above Arsenal in the race for the Champions League positions. In front of Sarina Wiegman, too.

Recent findings suggest that but Earps and London City also managed to ensure that Arsenal’s miserable wait without a home win this season continued, with five successive draws at the Emirates to begin their campaign. It will be little consolation to Renee Slegers that her side showed more intent and direction that in their previous draws against Crystal Palace, Manchester United, Birmingham City and Aston Villa this season: this was billed as a must-win for Arsenal and the sight of the goalkeeper Misa Rodriguez going forward for a corner in the final seconds of stoppage time, at 1-1, revealed as much.

That Arsenal’s corner failed to even reach the box, with Smilla Holmberg’s outswinging delivery instead drifting out of play, summed up how perplexing their season has become. A team who started the season with title aspirations, to go along with the club’s wider ambitions, are left sitting sixth in the WSL after 10 games, 12 points off leaders Chelsea and six points off London City, the holders of the final Champions League place. Arsenal are simultaneously a team capable of going to Barcelona and the Camp Nou on Wednesday and drawing 1-1, while also failing to register a victory in front of the biggest women’s football crowd in the country in the last six months.

In a way, London City were the sort of opponents Arsenal should have enjoyed facing. The plucky upstarts, with the billionaire owner and Ballon d’Or holder in midfield, are expansive in possession and have interesting ideas about what to do on the ball. They arrived at the Emirates with a plan and ambition to do more than just nullify their opponents and it was a measure of their ability to dictate that Arsenal, at times, did not even attempt to press. London City had more possession and more passes, which for Arsenal at least allowed them to break out of the sterile, side-to-side patterns of play that had defined their previous stalemates here.

It has been revealed that and there was a reminder, too, that Arsenal can be dangerous when they are presented with space, to attack in a way where they can move up the pitch and have a shot within seconds. Earps was kept busy, after all, and a lot of Arsenal managed to find made sense, at last: using Alessia Russo’s ability to work the channels and her awareness to bring others into play, looking to release Lisa Baum on the right and instructing her to be direct when she had a clear line to goal.

Maanum’s goal, after just 10 minutes, was an example of that. Emily Fox was invited to drive forwards and was directed to find Russo’s bending run off the shoulder of the last defender. There was a synchronisation to the way Russo didn’t even need to look up to know that Maanum would be arriving on the edge of the box, if she could find the right angle on the pull-back. There was a sense to Slegers leaving Olivia Smith and many of her summer signings on the bench and trusting the understanding between players like Russo and Maanum.

Sources indicate that but then Arsenal this season have usually displayed a way of shooting themselves in the foot, too. As Maanum celebrated and her team-mates huddled around her, Leah Williamson was pointing to her head and telling them they still needed to stay switched on. Yet within 98 seconds London City were level due to a moment, a glitch in the system. It came from Williamson, failing to match Izzy Goodwin’s run, stepping in at the wrong time in the box. The England captain was horribly bypassed by a centre-forward who offered a sharp contrast by simply being in total control of what she was doing.

According to recent reports, the frustration from Arsenal is their errors keep piling on top of each other, the scrutiny too. It is now just three wins from 10 in the WSL. Earps, in her defiance, sensed her opportunity to ensure there would be no respite.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Metalcore band Bleed From Within have designed Clyde's upcoming third kit.

The former Liverpool manager Jurgen Klopp once described the high-octane style of his teams as "heavy metal football.".

Now Scottish League Two side Clyde have gone a step further than Klopp's metaphor - by agreeing a sponsorship deal with a rock band.

Metalcore act Bleed From Within have also co-designed the newly introduced third kit for the club nicknamed "the Bully Wee", who now play in the band's home town of Hamilton, South Lanarkshire.

The group, who have released seven albums, said the new partnership was "an opportunity not to be missed".

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland.

The band's singer Scott Kennedy said: "Working with Clyde FC was a no brainer.

"Given our shared connections to Glasgow, where we played our first highlights and Hamilton, where the band was formed, we knew this made sense.

"We couldn't be happier with how the shirts turned out and we look forward to supporting the guys throughout the season and beyond.".

The new shirt features colour tones from the group's 2020 record Fracture and is designed to appeal to "communities in football and music".

Clyde chief executive David Alexander noted: "We are beyond excited to work with Bleed From Within on our third shirt for the 26/27 season.

"As a club who thrive on living outside the box and doing things differently, we had no hesitation when given the option to team up with an iconic name in the metal industry from Glasgow.

"A number of staff members already familiar with the artist, gave immediate excitement at the potential to turn heads and raise visibility of the club through such a great band.".

Alexander added that since the project was floated the club had "enjoyed watching the band storm across the European festival circuit".

Wet Wet Wet sponsored Clydebank in 1993.

Bleed From Within worked on the shirt design with Clyde's technical partner Terrace, who said the group had shown great enthusiasm for the idea.

The band join a long line of music acts who have become involved with football clubs.

Ed Sheeran - who was also a minority owner of the club - sponsored Ipswich Town for four seasons, starting in 2021.

Last year rock band Franz Ferdinand backed youth football team Symington Tinto 2014s, with the group's logo appearing on kits.

In October US rock band Wheatus agreed to sponsor a Worcestershire youth football team.

And in the 1990s Clydebank were sponsored by the pop band Wet Wet Wet, who came from the West Dunbartonshire town.

Other acts like the Libertines, Fontaines D.C and Mogwai have also been involved in sponsorship of teams in the past.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After six years in Italy and Scotland, Paul Gascoigne returned to English football in March 1998 when he signed for Middlesbrough.

At this stage of his career, Gazza was no longer the force of nature that lit up Italia 90 and Euro 96 as he body struggled to keep up the pace with his footballing brain.

However, his ability to be at the centre of attention and to entertain all around him, remained undiminished.

Former Boro goalkeeper Mark Schwarzer had a front row seat for all of Gazza’s pranks and hijinks - whether they lit up the dressing room, or left team-mates seeing red.

“Gazza has a heart of gold,” Schwarzer tells FourFourTwo. “All he wants to do is make people laugh, have fun and bring smiles to people’s faces.

“He’d do stuff that was outrageously funny and wrong, but there was never any malice.”.

When Gascoigne arrived at the Riverside Stadium, he joined from Rangers at the tail end of a campaign which had seen him score just three goals in 28 games and while his impact had clearly diminished from his early ‘90s pomp, it was clear to Schwarzer that the ability was still there.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“On the pitch, he highlighted glimpses of the player he had been, but there was frustration because his mind wanted to do things his body couldn’t always keep up with,” he continues.

“What a player, though, and what a person to be around.”.

As well as Gazza the player, the Boro squad also saw Gazza the character.

“Sometimes he’d come into training wearing the same clothes for days,” Schwarzer continues.

“One day, he took his socks off and went “Oh my God, these are horrendous”, then found Gianluca Festa’s Armani ones and swapped them for his own. Festa came back, realised what he’d done and started running around the building looking for him.

It has been revealed that “When Festa exploded, he exploded, but he couldn’t find Gazza, thank goodness. Festa ended up going home with no socks, because there was no way he was wearing Gazza’s!”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

England hold out, for a raucous win that will rightly be held up. Sure, it might not have been what it could have been as Ben White surged in for a sensational third in Madrid… but that last word remains key.

England beat the world and European champions 3-2 in their own capital, to end the longest unbeaten run in international history, that stretched back to March 2024.

Spain couldn’t make it 44 games, as England just about made it to 94 minutes. That was ultimately down to a brilliant double save from James Trafford, who was one of many positives on another Nations League night of enjoyably entertaining drama. Might Jordan Pickford’s first place have gone with Spain’s unbeaten run?

Sources indicate that trafford had to show his best. This was never going to be easy, no matter how Thomas Tuchel’s side made it look for 63 minutes - until Elliot Anderson’s red card. That will be the manager’s main takeaway from the game, the “proof of concept” as he put it the night before. With 11 against 11, England were denying this Spanish team the ball and creating some swift chances that the world champions were struggling to live with.

That was what the game-opening goal came from. Even if there was also debate about Anderson’s follow-through in that instance, England had opened another gap in the Spanish structure while looking so more cohesive and coruscating themselves.

Recent findings suggest that this is a team that can sustain attacking waves much better than the one who mostly forced their way through the summer on individual impact. White’s supreme goal, that had the world champions looking at each other and pointing fingers, was the grand exhibition of that.

In a recent development, just as crucially, it was so different to what Spain do. It was something of England's own. In between, Ezri Konsa scored the plundered set-piece header that his recent performances have deserved. Jude Bellingham was at that point bossing the Spanish midfield, in the kind of way people have long imagined as his career has only escalated.

This, and the very confidence from such a marker of a win, are what England have to take through to finally win that trophy at Euro 2028.

So many positives, so many solutions… until Spain asked the most severe questions, and Tuchel didn’t always have the answers. That is where there is obvious context to a win that should still inspire confidence.

It clearly meant much more to England given the fact Spain are the world champions who had won at Wembley. They're the ones who have done it, the benchmark. Tuchel and all the players were aware they had to do something more, to close this year with a performance that offered more for the future; that they had to stand up.

They had admittedly felt frustration from that Wembley defeat; that they could have won. As a consequence, England just looked sharper for pretty much all of the first hour. Spain didn’t even have a shot on target in the first half, as Unai Simon immediately had to withstand an England flurry.

The world champions weren’t counter-pressing in the way they were in the summer. England were starting to overrun them. The ultimate expression of that, in White’s goal, did seem to spark something in response.

It is possible that England themselves even got a bit overconfident. In what has been a theme in this double of games - that ended 3-2 apiece but see England top the group on goal difference - Tuchel’s side gave the ball away for a Spanish goal.

This time it was Anthony Gordon, who seemed to forget what Lamine Yamal can do. Even the Barcelona playmaker took a poor touch from there, leading to what felt like a needless challenge from Anderson. He was sent off, and Spain were set off.

It was immediately a different game. Spain were doing everything they weren’t in the first half. A change of midfield helped, with Fermin Lopez offering the impetus that Luis De La Fuente’s midfield had been missing. Nico Williams’s brilliant finish from an utterly sensational Yamal pass was then a goal to match White’s.

And so, in what was almost humorous irony, England ended 2026 in the way they’d ended its defining games: backs to the wall, a backline of nine, Tuchel hauling off his best attackers, and questions about the subs.

Spain really pressed. Yamal was at the heart of every move, creating almost every chance. The game then seemed to just constantly be the ball being fired across the England box. England were probably one bad bounce away from another inquest about Tuchel’s substitutions, and how he manages these matches.

But that bounce didn’t come. The equaliser didn't come. England stood up.

Recent findings suggest that and that might be because of a decision Tuchel doesn’t even have to make. Trafford made his claim. England made their mark.

It has been revealed that tuchel has ultimately overseen their most significant win for some time, at least as regards what it means for finally winning that trophy. That’s what all this is about, after all.

Sources indicate that spain can fairly say that what really matters is what happens in tournaments, but it didn’t feel meaningless as they toiled to keep that unbeaten record and the Madrid crowd willed them on. That run is now over. Might that finally signal that this could be England’s time?

It has been revealed that it is far too early to say, but this was the end to the year Tuchel wanted. It was the performance England needed.

If someone would've said to me I'd be doing this as a job when I was 12, I wouldn't have believed them.

In a recent development, my name's Jacob. I'm a content creator, and I work with Bolton Wanderers.

Industry observers note that my role here at Bolton is coming up with new ideas for social media, to try new concepts, filming stuff, and then posting them onto Bolton's pages and trying to help people follow the club. In my opinion, I think it's one of the funnest jobs in football, and it's brilliant.

Right. Welcome to Bolton, Larra. I hope I stated that right. I'm going to teach you some Bolton twang to help you settle in.

It has been revealed that my passion for football when I was growing up started at a very young age. My dad used to take me to the football matches, and I got my very first season ticket when I was five years old in the 2010/11 season, when Bolton was in the Premiership. Being something I loved as a kid, to turn it into my job is amazing.

I work here at least two days a week, obviously filming content, producing content,and then on match day, I'll be filming mostly with fans, and I love it.

In a recent development, as a town? Well, for us, it's lovely. Yeah.

Recent findings suggest that mondays, meetings. We have the marketing meeting, so that gives you an idea of what the week holds, what I'm going to do on a match day with the fans. And then in the week, I either film in with players, retail, commercial,whatever department needs help producing videos.

Some of the skills I use, I think one of them's got to be communication. You've got to be able to talk to people, talk to fans, and if you're watching this and you're a bit shy, or you think you can't communicate with people as well, I was like that inhigh school, so you learn it as you get older. But working in football, you've got to be adaptable because one minute you're doing a latest signing, next minute you're working with the players, next minute it's a match day, next minute the season's over.

Recent findings suggest that I'd say another one is being creative. That's probably the most vital one because without being creative, you won't be able to put a video together.

So when I was 16 in high school, that's where my journey started. I did videos, which got me a number of followers. I always struggled in the classroom side in high school, but creating content and creating ideas and being creative, I was always really, really good at in high school, whether that would be doing something drama-related or English, writing, creating stories. I always knew I had a passion for creative pieces of work and being able to now do it as a job, it suits me down to the ground.

In a recent development, I didn't go to college. I didn't go to uni. I left high school with no GCSEs, but I've always had a real passion for football, so that's how I got in contact with Bolton Wanderers. I started doing some videos here at Bolton with the fans and that, and then it turned into going to the training ground and filming with the players, working with the commercial team, retail team, all the different departmentsaround the football club to eventually getting a paid role in football.

In a recent development, I think don't wait for an opportunity to come to you. Get out there and try. If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role there. The highlight of my career so far, probably looking back, being resilient enough to create my own career path in doing something I love.

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

He's a content creator for Bolton Wanderers FC, coming up with new ideas for social media, filming videos and posting them onto official pages. The aim is to encourage people to follow the club.

There are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms.

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:.

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator.

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he states. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities.".

In a recent development, jacob indicates salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

Find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.
